newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan withdraws challenge to Islamic court rule.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan withdraws challenge to Islamic court rule.

text.p: Pakistan's government on Tuesday withdrew a challenge to an Islamic court ruling that had declared its interest-based Islamic banking un-Islamic, but asked for guidance on how to meet complex financial obligations.
The government withdrew its appeal that lay pending before the Supreme Court for almost five years against the judgment of the lower Federal Shariat Court, a government spokesman said.

But he said the government had filed a new application before the Shariat Court seeking its guidance "for enabling the government to fulfil its obligations in the light of Koran and Sunnah (practices of the Prophet Mohammad)".

The Shariat Court ruling in November, 1991, had rejected 32 financial laws it says are not sufficiently Islamic, including one that supplies the framework for mark-up, an Islamic alternative to interest payments by borrowers that has proved compatible with Western banking.
The court had given the government six months to November 11, 1992, to change the banking system, or appeal.

The government's appeal to the Supreme Court called the Shariat Court interpretation of the Koran incorrect and said the changes sought "will result in chaos and confusion" and financial institutions could not withstand them in the present circumstances.

It also said it was mandatory for the government to honour its internal and external fiscal obligations unless a suitable alternative was found and pleaded that the present system should continue until a workable alternative was found.
Then Islamic Democratic Alliance government of pime minister Nawaz Sharif had previously postponed an appeal because of pressure from fundamentalist allies in his coalition.

However, the religious parties quit the alliance later in 1992, leaving the way open for a government appeal, which Sharif's new government has now withdrawn 19 week after taking office following the February elections.

The new application has sought "authoritative answers and a workable solution which will prevent the government from being an international defaulter while remaining firmly within the framework of Islamic injunctions", the spokesman said.
Foreign bankers have said most of the laws the Shariat Court rejected had little or no impact on commerical banking.
The crucial ruling was against mark-up, which the court said was still too close to riba, or interest, which orthodox Moslems equate with usury and which is outlawed by Islam.

Under mark-up theory, introduced when Pakistan pioneered Islamic banking in the mid-1980s, the bank purchases whatever the lender requires. The lender then gradually buys the goods from the bank, paying mark-up charges for administration.
